text: Controls on the hydrogen isotopic composition of biogenic methane from high-latitude terrestrial wetlands
Jeffrey P. Chanton,1 Dana Fields,1 and Mark E. Hines2
Received 11 November 2005; revised 30 March 2006; accepted 9 June 2006; published 20 October 2006.

[1] To investigate the controls on the D isotopic composition of biogenic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ in terrestrial wetlands, we collected a series of samples for $\mathrm { \bar { \delta D } \mathrm { - } H _ { 2 } O , \delta D \mathrm { - } C \bar { H } _ { 4 } , \delta ^ { 1 3 } C \mathrm { - } C H _ { 4 } , }$ and $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - D I C }$ (dissolved $\Sigma C O _ { 2 } )$ along a N-S transect across Alaska from $6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N }$ to $7 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N }$ latitude from 7 to 15 August 2001. The $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ values varied from 108% to 161% and from 308% to 394%, respectively, from south to north and were significantly correlated, indicating the significant influence of the $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ on the D of terrestrial $\mathrm { { C H } _ { 4 } }$ collected along a latitudinal spatial gradient. Additionally, the apparent fractionation factors $( \alpha , \alpha _ { \mathrm { { A - B } } } = \mathrm { { R _ { A } } / \mathrm { { R _ { B } } , } }$ where $\mathrm { R } = { } ^ { \overleftarrow { 1 3 } } \mathrm { C } / { } ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { C }$ or D/H) for $\mathrm { \bar { H } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }  \mathrm { \bar { C } H } _ { 4 } ( \alpha _ { \mathrm { D } } )$ and $\mathrm { D I C } \longrightarrow \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \left( \alpha _ { \mathrm { C } } \right)$ varied from 1.26 to 1.42 and from 1.035 to 1.084, respectively, and were inversely correlated. We conclude that while $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ is a critical factor controlling $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ across latitudes, the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanism is also responsible for variation in the $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 } .$ If the isotopic values of the precursors of methane, $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , DIC, and organic matter are relatively constant, $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ produced by acetate fermentation will be enriched in $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and depleted in D relative to $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ produced via the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction pathway. Production mechanism variation will be particularly important in controlling variations in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ isotopic composition with depth. The strong dependence of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ on the D of environmental $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ indicates that specific fields on plots of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ versus $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ may not always accurately represent the isotopic composition of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ produced by $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction in northern wetlands. Because of this variation at high latitude, we assert that $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ values cannot be associated with production mechanism in an absolute sense. 1. Introduction

[2] Methane is the final end product of the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter. It is formed by two main pathways, acetate fermentation and reduction of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ with hydrogen. Variation in these two main mechanisms of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production has been hypothesized to be associated with inverse or antipathetic shifts in D and $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ [Whiticar et al., 1986; Schoell, 1988; Burke et $a l .$ , 1988a, 1988b; Whiticar, 1999; Hornibrook et al., 1997; Chanton et al., 2005]. It is often stated that fermentation of acetate will result in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ that is $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ enriched and D depleted relative to $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ produced via the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction pathway. Whiticar et al. [1986] defined somewhat distinct isotope compositional fields on a plot of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ versus $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ resulting from the different biogenic pathways and from thermogenic and geothermal origin. However, a portion of the D variation is due to variation in the precursor for CH4 hydrogen, which is in part $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { _ 2 O }$ . As discussed by Waldron et al. [1999], part of the reason for the D distinction between acetate-formed $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ versus $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ is because samples that were representative of the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction pathway were often from the marine environment where the $\delta \mathrm { D } \mathrm { - } \dot { \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ is close to $0 \text{‰}$ . Methane representative of acetate fermentation was more likely sampled from terrestrial environments where the $\delta \mathrm { D } \mathrm { - } \dot { \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ was somewhat depleted relative to marine $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ [Waldron et al., 1999]. For terrestrial environments at high latitudes, the effect will be more acute [Waldron et al., 1999].

[3] While the usefulness of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ as an indicator of methanogenic pathway has been recently demonstrated [e.g., Conrad et al., 2002; Sugimoto and Wada, 1993], the variation of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ with shifts in the acetate fermentation and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction pathways has been called into question [Waldron et al., 1999, 1998b; Sugimoto and Wada, 1995]. In several elegant experiments, investigators who have incubated organic matter of differing reactivity with $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { _ 2 O }$ of differing D isotopic composition [Sugimoto and $W a d a .$ 1995; Waldron et al., 1998a] have failed to observe shifts in the D of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ with changing production mechanism. What does appear to control the D of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ in these incubation studies is the D of $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ . The $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ values fall very close to a single line $( \mathrm { r } = 0 . 9 8 6 )$ when plotted against the $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ used in the experiment [Waldron et al., 1999].

[4] Waldron et al. [1999] also plotted 51 cogenetic pairs of $\partial \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ from environmental samples from a variety of environments across latitude. They obtained a significant relationship between $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and $\partial \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and concluded that the isotopic composition of formation $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ was the primary control on the $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ . They observed, however, that there was more variation for $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ than for $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ,$ , which might be caused by other processes. One of the purposes of this paper is to determine if variations in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production pathways might be one of these processes. Furthermore, the data of Waldron et al. [1999] was weighted toward more tropical and temperate areas. The authors suggested a need for additional data at higher latitudes.

[5] Chanton et al. [2005] presented results from field studies ranging from tropical to boreal regions and provided strong evidence that $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ produced from acetate fermentation is relatively $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ enriched and D depleted relative to $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ produced from reduction of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } .$ However, they pointed out that the relationship only holds if precursor isotopic values $( \delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - D I C }$ and $\delta \mathrm { D } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { \dot { H } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } )$ are relatively constant across the spatial or temporal gradients across which the measurements are made.

[6] In this paper we will examine field data to provide evidence that although precursor $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { _ 2 O }$ isotopic composition is a primary factor controlling the $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 } ,$ variations in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanisms are a second controlling factor. Therefore along a N-S transect across Alaska we measured D and $\delta ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { O }$ of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } , \delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and D of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ of DIC. Our first objective was to determine if fractionation of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ varies with $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanism by examining the variation of apparent fractionation factors for the pairs $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - D I C }$ and $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { { C H } _ { 4 } }$ and D-H2O and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 } .$ . To accomplish this we sampled semisynoptically across a horizontal gradient at different scales and synoptically along a depth gradient. Methane production mechanisms have been observed to vary as a function of depth in northern wetlands [Hornibrook et al., 1997; Chasar et al., 2000a, 2000b; Chanton et al., 2005]. Our second objective was to extend the observations of Waldron et al. [1999] by collecting additional data from a transect between 60 and 70 degrees north in Anchorage, Fairbanks and along the pipe line road in Alaska up to Deadhorse.
2. Methods

[7] Samples were collected from bogs and fens in Alaska along a latitudinal gradient, from boreal to polar regions (60.0 N to 69.5 N) and across a depth gradient at a single site. Sampling occurred from 7 to 15 August 2001 and represents a synoptic data set, not a seasonal study. Replicate samples of pore water were collected from depths ranging from 10 to 50 cm with a ‘‘swamp sucker,’’ which is a quarter inch stainless steel tube with holes drilled at the base combined with a 50 mL syringe. At Turnagain Bog, near Anchorage Alaska $( 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { { N } }$ latitude) in addition to shallow swamp sucker samples, additional samples were collected at depths ranging from 1 to 2 meters using a piezometer and a peristaltic pump. DIC (Dissolved Inorganic Carbon or $\sum \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ) .$ , samples were filtered through glass fiber filters and 10 mL injected into 25 mL evacuated serum vials fitted with butyl rubber septa. DIC samples were stored frozen and upside down prior to analysis and then acidified with 0.3 mL of degassed $3 0 \% \mathrm { ~ H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ and brought to ambient pressure through an open split tube with nitrogen for testing. Small subsamples $( 2 0 ~ \mu 1 )$ of the headspace from the DIC samples were run via direct injection on the GC-IRMS (HP-Finnigan Delta S) to determine $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - D I C }$ . For $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\delta \mathrm { { \bar { D } } - C H _ { 4 } }$ analysis, pore water was injected into evacuated 500 ml Qorpak brown glass bottles, containing 1.5 g KOH and stored upside down. Storage tests indicate that samples keep for over a year in this manner. Samples of $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ for isotopic analysis were placed within hypovials and stoppered with a needle fitted through the septae to allow a sample to be collected with no headspace. The needle was removed after the stopper was inserted.

[8] The headspaces of the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ samples were pressurized to one atmosphere with an open split tube and equilibrated with the dissolved phase. Then a small portion of each headspace was analyzed via direct injection into the GC-IRMS (Finnigan Delta S) to determine $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ and concentration. Methane from the rest of the headspace was removed with a helium stream and combusted over copper oxide at $8 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and the resultant $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { _ 2 O }$ and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ cryogenically trapped. The $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ from the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ combustion was isolated using an ethanol slush trap and transferred to glass tubes containing zinc shavings from Indiana University, which were then flame sealed. The tubes were heated to $5 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 minutes to react the $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ with the zinc and the resultant H2 was analyzed for $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ using the duel inlet system of the Finnigan MAT IRMS [Coleman et al., 1982]. D-CH4 was determined relative to Standard Mean Ocean Water (SMOW) using gases that were calibrated against standard waters (V-SMOW, SLAP). Precision for DD measurements on the IRMS is 0.3% while overall precision of replicate field samples is 6 % [Lombardi, 1999]. Samples of surface and pore water were sent to Waterloo University for analysis to determine the isotopic signatures of the pore water, $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and $\delta ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { O } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } .$ The $\ \overline { { { \delta } } } ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ values were determined relative to VPDB in %. Lab standards were calibrated against NIST standards. Precision for $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ measurements was ±0.2% on the basis of repeated measurements of a laboratory working standard.

We refer to these factors as apparent, because while $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { _ 2 O }$ are the precursors for $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ formed from $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction, they are not the immediate precursors for $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ formed from acetate fermentation. [15] Generally, the slope of the line of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ fit to $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ has been interpreted as being indicative of the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanism, with $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ generated purely from $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction having a slope of 1 because all of the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ hydrogen is thought to be derived from coexisting $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } .$ . Acetate fermentation is thought to have a slope of $0 . 2 5$ as only 1 hydrogen has been considered to be derived from environmental $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ while the other 3 have been thought to be transferred intact from the acetate methyl group [Whiticar, 1999; Whiticar et al., 1986]. Strict interpretation of the overall results (Figure 3b) in light of this paradigm would suggest a $6 0 { - } 4 0$ mix of acetate fermentation and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction in the generation of global terrestrial $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ as included in the data set. However, the picture is probably not so simple as it initially appeared to be [Waldron et $a l .$ , 1999]. Recent evidence has suggested that there may be an exchange of hydrogen between the acetate methyl group and $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ in the final stages of methanogenic acetate metabolism [de Graaf et al., 1996]. Presumably this isotopic exchange is accompanied by an isotopic fractionation but the magnitude of this effect has not been quantified, as pointed out by Hornibrook et al. [1998].

[16] Hydrogen concentration has also been suggested as a factor that may influence the isotopic composition of H in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \ [ B u r k e _ { \mathrm { ~ ; ~ } }$ , 1993; Sugimoto and Wada, 1995], and this factor may be particularly responsible for the lack of agreement between incubation studies and surveys of natural wetlands [Chanton et al., 2005]. Burke [1993] proposed that hydrogen concentration could affect the fractionation of H between H2O and $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } ,$ resulting in greater fractionation at higher H2 concentrations but not affecting the $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ Recently, Valentine $e t$ al. [2004] observed that microbial growth rate can have a profound effect on fractionation $( \alpha _ { \mathrm { D } } )$ between $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ and $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ during $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction, thus influencing the $\delta \mathrm { D }$ of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } .$ . Furthermore environmental $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ D variation affects the D of organic matter and thus should affect the D of the acetate methyl group. Given these uncertainties, it is best not to interpret the slope value too strictly. It can be suggested on the basis of Figures 3a and 3b that 50 to $70 \%$ of the variation in $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ is directly related to variation in D of environmental $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$

[17] It is interesting that the Alaska data set indicated a slope of 1.5 (Figure ${ 3 } \mathrm { a } ) ,$ , greater than what would have been expected for $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction alone. This finding could be due to variation with production mechanism with latitude in our data set. Lower-latitude $( 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N } )$ data were dominated by samples from Turnagain Bog where acetate is known to accumulate in interstitial water and not form $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ [Hines et al., 2001; Duddelston et al., 2002]. In general studies have been interpreted to indicate that CH4 production via the acetate pathway is less consequential in high-latitude Sphagnum-dominated bogs [Lansdown et al., 1992; Chasar et $a l .$ , 2000a, 2000b; Chanton et al., 2005]. Variation in radiocarbon distributions between DOC, $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } ,$ and DIC further support the idea that respiration modes fundamentally differ in bogs and fens [Chasar et al., 2000b]. Turnagain bog samples varied from 115% to 123% in $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ isotopic composition, and thus represented the right side of the graph in Figure 3a. Nonetheless the Turnagain data fit the line quite well. As most of the sites we sampled were represented by only 1 or 2 data, we investigated reducing the number of surface Turnagain data points to only two randomly chosen surface samples, samples 1 and $^ { 3 , }$ which are fairly representative of the other surface samples. This reduction changed the line fit to the data little, to $\mathbf { y } = 1 . 2 7 \mathrm { x } - 1 8 8 . 4 5 , \overset { \sim } { \mathrm { r } } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 5 9$ . Thus the possible overrepresentation of Turnagain Bog as a lower-latitude (60-) sampling site is not responsible for the observed pattern.

Our Alaska data had a more positive intercept than the overall data set, which might be interpreted as due to a greater influence of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction at higher latitudes because of the inhibition of the acetate fermentation pathway in Sphagnum-dominated bogs. [20] We next evaluate the hypothesis that departures from the linear fit observed in Figure 3a are related to variations in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanism. We will assume that variation in the signature of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ indicates variation in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanism, as discussed by Conrad et al. [2002] [see also Sugimoto and Wada, 1993; Waldron et $a l . ,$ 1998a], since samples were collected from depths that were for the most part $\dot { 2 } 5$ cm below the surface and thus should be relatively free of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ oxidation as was observed for northern wetlands by $P o p p$ et al. [1999]. When $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ is plotted versus $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { \bar { C } - C H _ { 4 } } ^ { \bullet } .$ an inverse correlation results (Figure 4), consistent with this assumption. If $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ was controlled by CH oxidation, a positive correlation between $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and D of CH4 would have been observed [Coleman et al., 1981; Chanton et $a l .$ , 2005]. Additionally, the finding of a negative correlation in Figure 4 is consistent with the hypothesis that some of the variation in D that we observed across our transect was due to variation in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanism. In Figure 4, there appear to be two clusters of data, those on the left where $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction is more important, and those on the right where acetate fermentation is more dominant. The left cluster data are from latitudes below $6 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N }$ and include data from Turnagain bog, where incubation studies have clearly demonstrated that $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction is the dominant production mechanism.

The right-side data are from above $6 4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N }$ . We suspect that this segregation of the data with latitude is serendipitous, and does not imply that there are variations in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production pathways with latitude on this scale. On larger latitudinal scales, however, for example in Sphagnum-dominated wetlands which are more often found in northern latitudes, one is likely to observe that $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ reduction is the dominate methane production mechanism. This finding has been observed in both isotopic and incubation studies [Landsdown et al., 1992; Chasar et al., 2000a, 2000b; Hines et al., 2001; Duddleston et $a l .$ , 2002].

[21] However, some portion of the variation in $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ in Figure 4 is caused by the variation in $\delta \mathrm { D } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ with latitude (Figure 3a). Assuming that the variation in $\bar { \delta } ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ is due to variation in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ production mechanism, then this finding is consistent with the hypothesis that $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ varies with production mechanism as well, in an opposite manner to $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 } .$ Thus it appears that variation in production mechanism is a second factor controlling the $\delta \mathrm { { D - C H } _ { 4 } . }$ .
